outcome: No proof or disproof that there are infinitely many amicable numbers has appeared since 26 January 2024, and the question is still stated as open in the Lean formalisations and in the 2026 papers that discuss it. The window does hold one event that bounds the counting function A(x) of integers lying in amicable pairs: Paul Pollack's arXiv:2610.05661 (5 October 2026), whose abstract says the proof was 'found by ChatGPT Astra'; it bounds A(x) from above and does not address infinitude. The other in-window items are a Lean formalisation (January 2026) that states but does not prove the question, an identity paper on pairs with power-of-two gcd (December 2025), generalisation papers (2024, 2025), and four geometric or knot papers that use the word 'amicable' in an unrelated sense.
problem_asks: (a) Whether the set of amicable numbers is infinite. The bullet asks for 'amicable numbers', not 'amicable pairs', and the two readings are equivalent here: each amicable number n has at most one partner, namely s(n), the sum of its proper divisors, so infinitely many amicable numbers means infinitely many amicable pairs. The bullet asks for no count, density, growth rate, parity, coprimality or size. Erdős problem 830, which the Wikipedia wording matches, also asks (b) whether A(x) > x^(1-o(1)) for the count of pairs up to x; that second question is not part of this bullet and is recorded here only so the judging pass can see the mapping. Note that erdosproblems.com/830 defines amicable as sigma(a)=sigma(b)=a+b with a<=b, which as written would admit a=b (perfect numbers) unless the formal IsAmicable excludes it; I did not check that.

events.what_happened: Kanold, a short contribution to the Proceedings of the International Congress of Mathematicians, Amsterdam 1954 ('Über die asymptotische Dichte von gewissen Zahlenmengen'), showing that the amicable numbers have upper asymptotic density below 0.204, i.e. that at most about 0.204x integers up to x lie in an amicable pair for large x. Known only through secondary citations (Erdős 1955 and Pomerance/Pollack expositions in search results); the 1954 text was not available to me.
events.delivers: An upper density bound (below 0.204) on the set of amicable numbers. It bounds the counting function A(x) from above only and says nothing about whether the set is infinite.
events.remains: Everything in problem_asks: infinitude of amicable numbers and of amicable pairs.
events.direction: Upper density bound, so amicable numbers are sparse. Cuts neither way on infinitude.
sources: https://static.renyi.hu/~p_erdos/1955-03.pdf (cites Kanold; PDF unreadable, reference seen in search snippet only)

events.what_happened: P. Erdős, 'On amicable numbers', Publicationes Mathematicae Debrecen 4 (1955), 108-111 (DOI 10.5486/PMD.1955.4.1-2.16). Proves that the amicable numbers have asymptotic density zero, A(x)=o(x), improving Kanold's bound. The argument uses the observation that in an amicable pair the smaller member is abundant and the larger deficient. Erdős also states a sharper bound of order x/log log log x (per secondary quotation). The paper's scan was unreadable to me; the content above comes from search snippets and later expositions, not the paper itself.
events.delivers: Zero asymptotic density for amicable numbers, A(x)=o(x). A density-zero set can still be infinite, so this does not settle the bullet.
events.remains: Infinitude of amicable numbers and pairs. Also the lower-bound question A(x) > x^(1-o(1)) recorded in problem_asks as the second part of Erdős 830, which this result does not touch.

The abstract (opened) gives a history of amicable numbers and a characterisation of amicable pairs whose gcd is a power of two, through distinct prime factorisations, for three shape families (2^n ab with 2^n cd; 2^n abc with 2^n de; 2^n abc with 2^n def), with identities relating phi(A)+phi(B) to the odd prime factors. The PDF body could not be read (compressed streams), so its theorems and any statement about the status of infinitude or about bounds are unverified. A search snippet attributes to it a statement that infinitude is still unknown; I could not confirm that.

events.what_happened: Z. Chen, H. Tang and J. Zhan (Shanghai Dianji University), 'Formalization of Amicable Numbers Theory', arXiv:2601.07444, submitted 12 January 2026 (one version). A 2076-line Lean 4 development against Mathlib, with 139 theorems and, per the authors, zero sorry placeholders. Formalises the definitions; complete proofs of Thābit's rule, Thābit's formula and Euler's generalised rule; the Borho-Hoffmann breeding method; sociable and betrothed numbers; some parity constraints; coprime search bounds; and Poulet's 5-cycle. Section 3.8 says the authors 'formalized three famous open problems as Lean definitions' (existence of odd-odd pairs, infinitude of amicable pairs, existence of coprime pairs) and that these 'provide clear goal statements for possible future proof efforts'. So the infinitude question appears as a Lean definition, not a theorem, and nothing is proved or disproved about it.
events.revisions: v1 only (12 Jan 2026), per arXiv abstract page.
events.delivers: Machine-checked proofs of generation rules and some parity and coprimality statements, plus a Lean definition of the infinitude question. None of these bears on whether the set is infinite.

The zero-sorry claim is therefore not reconciled with the text. No explicit sorry is shown in the text. No external reading or review was found.

events.what_happened: P. Pollack, 'Amicable numbers', arXiv:2610.05661 (11 pages; comment: 'expository article on AI-generated work'). One version. The arXiv abstract page gives submission on 5 October 2026 (01:15 UTC); the arXiv search listing gives 4 October 2026 for the same entry. Abstract, as returned by the HTML rendering and quoted by the tool: 'Let s(n):=sum of the proper divisors of n'; 'Distinct positive integers n,m form an amicable pair if s(n)=m and s(m)=n'; 'Let A(x) count the positive integers not exceeding x that belong to an amicable pair'; 'We report on a proof, found by ChatGPT Astra, that A(x)<=x exp{-(1/2+o(1)) log x log_3 x / log_2 x} as x tends to infinity.' The introduction says the proof 'was discovered by ChatGPT Astra'. The AI-usage statement says 'The proof of Theorem 1 was produced by ChatGPT Astra', that 'ChatGPT Astra also produced a Lean formalization of Theorem' 1, and that 'P.P. takes full responsibility for the mathematical content without claiming credit for discovering the proof'. The Lean repository the paper cites, github.com/twonth/amicable-numbers-lean (opened), has main theorem AmicableCertificate.amicable_count_upper_bound in Certificate.lean, which by the README's informal rendering says that for every real c<1/2 there is x0 such that A(x) <= x exp(-c log x log_3 x / log_2 x) for x >= x0. The README says the result was checked against Lean 4.35.0-rc3 and Mathlib, that the reported axioms are propext, Classical.choice and Quot.sound, and that the result passed the Lean Comparator against a Mathlib-only challenge; it credits 'ChatGPT Astra' for the formalisation; and it says 'This records the author's statement review, not a line-by-line human audit of all Lean proofs or independent peer review.' An intentional sorry in Challenge.lean specifies the question; the README says the checked solution does not depend on it. The bound is on A(x), a quantity the bullet does not name. It does not say whether infinitely many amicable numbers exist. On my own comparison of the two displayed formulas (not a claim in the source): the exponent (1/2) log x log_3 x / log_2 x exceeds Pomerance's (1/2) sqrt(log x log_3 x) by a factor that tends to infinity, so this is a stronger upper bound than the 2015 bound.
events.revisions: v1 only, 5 Oct 2026 per arXiv abstract page (listing shows 4 Oct 2026 for the same entry; a time-zone difference is the likely cause).
events.delivers: An upper bound on the counting function A(x) of the form x^(1-(1/2+o(1)) log_3 x / log_2 x), i.e. x^(1-o(1)) with an explicit o(1). Restricted to the counting function. It gives no lower bound on A(x), and no statement about whether infinitely many amicable numbers exist. Its scale matches the x^(1-o(1)) question that is the second part of Erdős 830, which is not part of this bullet; the record does not decide what, if anything, it does to that part.
events.remains: Whether there are infinitely many amicable numbers (problem_asks (a)); also any lower bound on A(x).
events.directly_checkable: The bound itself is an analytic statement about A(x) and was not checked by hand. The Lean statement AmicableCertificate.amicable_count_upper_bound in Certificate.lean is the checkable object; I read only the README, did not read the source, and did not build the repository.
events.doubts: (1) No external human engagement was found in six days; the only human named is the author, who says he takes responsibility without claiming to have discovered the proof. (2) The README explicitly says it is not a line-by-line human audit or independent peer review. (3) Build-level claims (kernel check, axioms, Comparator, 'no sorry' for the solution) rest on the author's README; I did not reproduce them. The repository has an intentional sorry in Challenge.lean. (4) The repository lists about 110 Lean files and the results table names two files absent from the visible listing; 11 commits are shown with no dates. (5) The credited author of the Lean repository is 'twonth'; I did not establish who that is. (6) The paper credits ChatGPT Astra with both the proof and the formalisation, so as far as the sources show, no human has read the argument as a mathematician's proof; the text says the author takes full responsibility, which is not an independent check.
events.direction: Cuts toward sparseness of amicable numbers (an upper bound on A(x)). Neither proves nor refutes infinitude.

systems.name: ChatGPT Astra
systems.what_it_did: Per the paper, found the proof of the upper bound on A(x) (Theorem 1) and produced a Lean formalisation of Theorem 1. Press coverage (Quanta, 3 Aug 2026, opened) describes Astra as an unreleased OpenAI model; the paper's own name for it is 'ChatGPT Astra', and its pre-release status comes from press coverage, not the paper. The author states they take responsibility for the mathematical content and do not claim to have discovered the proof.

summary: The question has not been moved: no proof or refutation of infinitude has appeared since January 2024, and every source I read that discusses it still calls it open or states it as a Lean definition only. I searched for the problem under its names and with proof, counterexample and bound terms, and ran a separate AI search. The search turned up one event I did not expect: arXiv:2610.05661, posted by Paul Pollack on 5 October 2026 and listed as 4 October in the arXiv search. Its abstract reports an upper bound A(x) <= x exp(-(1/2+o(1)) log x log_3 x / log_2 x) for the count of integers lying in amicable pairs, and says the proof was 'found by ChatGPT Astra'. The paper repeats that the proof of Theorem 1 was 'produced by ChatGPT Astra', and that the same system produced a Lean formalisation; the author says he takes responsibility for the mathematics without claiming to have discovered it. The cited repository's README states the formal statement, the axioms and a Comparator run, and says it is not a human audit. I could not read the paper body. The bound is a real counting result, but the bullet asks only whether infinitely many amicable numbers exist, and a bound on A(x) leaves that open, so on my reading it does not change the problem's status. Two readings are close. Under the broader reading that Erdős 830 includes its second part, the bound sits on the same x^(1-o(1)) scale as that part's lower-bound question, so it bears on that question without deciding it. Under the bullet's own wording it does not bear. The older bounds (Kanold 1954, Erdős 1955, Pomerance 1981 and 2015, Nguyen and Pomerance 2019) and the in-window papers (Dimitrov 2024 and 2025, Euler's translation, the Mavaddat and Alikhani identities, the Lean formalisation of January 2026, the AlphaProof Nexus campaign and four geometric or knot papers named 'amicable') are recorded as events and discounted with reasons. I checked the AI side in three ways. The AlphaProof Nexus campaign, which covered 353 Erdős problems and 492 OEIS conjectures, does not list problem 830 among the attempts, and the 38 released OEIS proofs contain no amicable-related A-number. The OEIS Open benchmark's full text contains only one 'amicable' hit, A272479, a Harshad-amicable sequence. Searches for Claude, Gemini, GPT, Aristotle, AlphaEvolve and FunSearch with amicable turned up nothing else. Where sources disagree, I have kept both readings. The Pomerance 2015 bound appears in three forms across the Erdős database, the Lean file and a December 2025 preprint. Wikipedia's parity sentence ('either both even or both odd') differs from the Lean paper's ('both members are even'). The known pair count is 'over 1 billion' in Wikipedia (retrieved 28 May 2024) and 'over 1.2 billion' in the Lean paper; a count of pairs is not a step toward infinitude, so I did not record it as an event.
competing_reading: The strongest case against my reading is that the Pollack bound is the first event in the record that moves a quantity the problem is about: the counting function of the amicable set, which Erdős 830 part (ii) and the usual heuristic (more than x^(1-epsilon) pairs up to x) both use. Under that reading the bound is a real step, and the AI attribution is load-bearing. Against it: the bullet asks only whether infinitely many amicable numbers exist, a question an upper bound on A(x) leaves untouched whatever its size, and the upper bound is the wrong direction for the heuristic that would support infinitude. A second reading: the Lean certificate's checks, if they hold, make the bound more secure than the 2015 bound, which was never machine-checked; but the README is the author's own statement and was not reproduced here.
what_would_settle_it: For the bullet's question, only a proof or refutation of infinitude, and none has appeared. For the Pollack event: (1) the full text of arXiv:2610.05661, to read the paper's own comparison with Pomerance 2015 and any statement on infinitude, and the wording of the AI-usage statement; (2) a local build of github.com/twonth/amicable-numbers-lean to confirm the axioms and the absence of sorry in the solution, and the Lean statement against Theorem 1; (3) any later reading or review, and any OpenAI account of Astra's output. For the AI campaign: the full list of the 44 AlphaProof Nexus OEIS results, including the six not released, and the list of the Gemini evaluation of 700 open conjectures in Bloom's database reported by Quanta, to confirm whether any amicable-related conjecture or problem 830 was included. For the 2015 bound: the Springer chapter's Theorem 1.1, to settle the form of the bound.
